input: In this worked example, our goal is to calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction, and also to work out what fraction of the reactant remains after a period of 60 min has elapsed. For a first-order reaction, the rate constant k (in units of min-1) determines the half-life t1/2 (in min) through the simple relationship t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction of the reactant that remains after a time t (in min) is given by exp(-k t). In the case we are considering here, the measured rate constant is k = 0.046 min-1 at a temperature of 323 K, and this value was obtained from concentration measurements that were taken every 5 min over a total period of 90 min. Substituting the value of k into the half-life formula, we find that the half-life is 15.1 min, which means that the amount of reactant falls to half of its value every 15.1 min. Moving on to the second part of the problem, we can substitute k = 0.046 min-1 and t = 60 min into the decay expression, and this gives us a fraction remaining after 60 min of 0.06, which means that only a small proportion of the original material is still present at that point. The fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.06 because the interval spans several half-lives: with a half-life of 15.1 min, successive halvings reduce the amount step by step until a fraction of 0.06 is left. It is important to bear in mind that these particular relationships are valid for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of a different order would follow a different decay law, and the same formulas would not apply to it.
target: The half-life of the reaction is 15.1 min, and the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.06. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). The measured rate constant is k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Substitution in the half-life relation with k = 0.046 min-1 gives the half-life as 15.1 min. Substitution in exp(-k t) with the same rate constant and t = 60 min gives the fraction remaining after 60 min as 0.06 (dimensionless). The two results read together state the decay plainly: the amount halves every 15.1 min, so an interval of 60 min contains several successive halvings, and the fraction left at the end of it (0.06) is correspondingly small. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only. A reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither the half-life relation nor the exponential fraction applies to it; the half-life of such a reaction is not fixed by the rate constant alone in this way, and it changes as the reaction proceeds. Both results come from the one measured rate constant, and each can be checked against the other before either is used.
